statement: In people in the USA who stopped taking prescribed tramadol in its first five years on the market (April 1995 to March 2000), withdrawal was reported, mostly as ordinary opioid withdrawal and, in about 1 in 8 reported cases, with symptoms not usual in opioid withdrawal, such as severe anxiety and panic, confusion or feelings of unreality, numbness or tingling, and hallucinations; these are reported cases only, with no comparison group, so how often withdrawal follows stopping tramadol, and whether it differs from withdrawal from other opioids measured the same way, are not known. A committee that the manufacturer set up on the recommendation of an FDA advisory committee classified 1,248 adverse-event reports that reached the company or the FDA, or a paid network of 255 drug researchers, clinicians and counsellors (average response 48.7%), using ratings based on DSM-IV (Senay et al., 2003). Withdrawal was rated only where there was no drug-seeking: 422 reports (33 in 100 of all reports by Table 3; the abstract says nearly 40), of which 367 were 'typical', with at least three DSM-IV opioid withdrawal symptoms such as stomach cramps, diarrhoea, goose flesh, a runny nose, sweating, restlessness and poor sleep, and 55 'atypical' (13 in 100 of withdrawal reports, about 1 in 8): opioid-type withdrawal with a strong component of other symptoms. Among these 55, severe anxiety and panic attacks were reported in 32.8%, confusion, delusions, depersonalization, derealization or paranoia in 27.2%, numbness, tingling or ringing in the ears in 25.4%, and hallucinations of touch, sight or hearing in 20.0%. Another 124 reports, rated as 'abuse' because of drug-seeking, also described withdrawal (121 typical, 3 atypical), so at least 546 reports described it. Of typical cases with a known dose (63 in 100), 92 in 100 had taken at most 400 mg a day, which the authors give as the maximum recommended dose (range 50 to 2,000 mg), and many cases followed only 3 or 4 days of use (exposure known for about half; no counts); a quarter of atypical cases (dose known for 78 in 100) had taken more than 400 mg a day, against 8 in 100 of typical cases (no counts or test). Withdrawal followed sudden stopping, which the authors say many doctors did despite the label's warning, and in some cases a gradual reduction. Doctors described most reported cases as mild and usually over in 2 or 3 days, and the committee says atypical cases tended to last longer and to be harder to manage (no counts; it also drew on about 75 consultations). The authors say the atypical symptoms resembled those reported on stopping SSRI antidepressants more than opioid withdrawal, suggest, without testing it, a link with tramadol's effects on serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake, and warn that they could be mistaken for psychosis or delirium; apart from the higher doses, they found nothing that told who would have them. Limits: the cases are reports someone chose to make, with no count of the people who stopped without withdrawal and no group stopping another opioid; the reporting rate peaked at about 2.3 reported cases per 100,000 people estimated to have been prescribed tramadol in a quarter (read from the figure; 2.5 to 3.0 in the text) and later fell below 1, the authors also give about 1 and under 2 per 100,000, and they cite an FDA estimate that spontaneous reports capture only about 10 in 100 adverse events and say that after several years they probably capture well under 5 in 100, so these rates are minimums, not how often withdrawal happens; age was known for 139 of 455 cases (a total that matches neither 422 nor 546), sex for 82 to 87 in 100 (about 56 in 100 of them women) and the dose for 63 to 78 in 100; other medicines, antidepressants among them, and earlier drug use were not reported; the 'atypical' category was created during the study and every case was rescored, with no check of agreement between raters, and it is described both as always coming with typical symptoms and as sometimes replacing them; reports with drug-seeking were counted as 'abuse', not withdrawal; no statistical test is reported; and the work was funded by a grant from the manufacturer, and the article has no conflict-of-interest statement. A systematic review of Iranian studies (Rostam-Abadi et al., 2020) describes two case reports of tramadol withdrawal: a man who sought help with mental and physical symptoms 2 weeks after suddenly stopping tramadol he had taken for 2 years, all gone within a few days (its reference list titles the report as psychosis following tramadol withdrawal), and a newborn with vomiting, poor feeding, tremor and seizures whose mother had taken tramadol for back pain during pregnancy; it describes no study of how often withdrawal follows stopping tramadol. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Is tramadol withdrawal different from other opioids? Sometimes, going by reports. Of 1,248 side-effect reports from tramadol's first five years in the US (1995 to 2000), 422 described withdrawal after stopping, without signs of drug-seeking. Most looked like ordinary opioid withdrawal, with symptoms such as cramps, diarrhoea, goose bumps, a runny nose, sweating and poor sleep. About 1 in 8 (55) also had symptoms not usual in opioid withdrawal: severe anxiety or panic, confusion or feeling unreal, numbness or tingling, or hallucinations. The researchers say these looked more like stopping an SSRI antidepressant and could be mistaken for psychosis. Most people whose dose was known had taken no more than the recommended daily maximum, many had used tramadol for only a few days, and doctors described most cases as mild and over in 2 or 3 days. But these are only cases someone chose to report: the researchers cite an estimate that only about 1 in 10 side effects get reported, and nobody compared people stopping tramadol with people stopping other opioids, so how often withdrawal happens, and how it compares, is unknown. The drug's maker paid for the study. A review of Iranian studies found only two case reports, one of them a newborn whose mother had taken tramadol in pregnancy.
population: People in the USA prescribed tramadol (Ultram) in its first five years on the market (April 1995 to March 2000) whose withdrawal after stopping or reducing it was reported to the manufacturer, the FDA (MedWatch) or a paid network of 255 drug researchers, clinicians and counsellors; in Iran, two case reports (an adult and a newborn)
exposure: Stopping tramadol, mostly suddenly and in some reports gradually (reported daily amounts, where known, 50–2,000 mg in typical and 50–1,300 mg in atypical cases)
comparator: None: no people who stopped tramadol without withdrawal and no people stopping another opioid; 'typical' and 'atypical' reports compared descriptively, 'atypical' defined against the DSM-IV list of opioid withdrawal symptoms
outcome: Withdrawal as classified by the committee from reports: 'typical' opioid withdrawal (at least three DSM-IV opioid withdrawal symptoms, no drug-seeking) and 'atypical' withdrawal (opioid-type withdrawal with other nervous-system symptoms); the share of each symptom group among atypical cases; reported cases per 100,000 people estimated to be prescribed
magnitude: Senay et al. (2003), adverse-event reports from April 1995 to March 2000: 1,248 classified; 422 rated withdrawal without drug-seeking (Table 3: 33%; editors' calculation 33.8%; abstract and Discussion: nearly 40%): typical 367 (86.97%), atypical 55 (13.03%; about 1 in 8; typical to atypical about 7 to 1); of 644 reports rated as 'abuse', 124 also had withdrawal symptoms (121 typical, 3 atypical), at least 546 in all (43.8% of 1,248, editors' calculation). Among the 55 atypical: severe anxiety and panic 32.8%, unusual CNS symptoms 27.2%, unusual sensory phenomena 25.4%, hallucinations 20.0% (as printed; the nearest counts of 55 give 32.7%, 27.3%, 25.5% and 20.0%, editors' calculation; the total exceeds 100%). Dose known in 63% of typical cases (50–2,000 mg a day; 92% at or below 400 mg) and 78% of atypical cases (50–1,300 mg; 25% above 400 mg, against 8% of typical; no counts); exposure known in about 50%, many of 3–4 days (no counts). Reporting rate per 100,000 people estimated to be prescribed: peak about 2.3 in the quarter centred on May 1996 (37 typical, 10 atypical reports; read from Figure 1), 2.5–3.0 in the text; later below 1 (last quarter about 0.3); approximately 1 (p. 238) and less than 2 (p. 239) in the Discussion; capture of spontaneous reports cited as about 10%, later under 5%. Sex known in 82% and 87%, about 56% women. Rostam-Abadi et al. (2020): two Iranian case reports (an adult; a newborn); no study of withdrawal frequency.

evidence.extracted: Post-marketing surveillance by an independent steering committee that the drug's sponsor, Ortho-McNeil Pharmaceuticals, set up on the recommendation of the FDA's Drug Abuse Advisory Committee when tramadol (Ultram) was marketed in the USA without scheduling. Reports came from spontaneous adverse-event reports to the company and the FDA (MedWatch: patients, pharmacists, physicians) and from a network of 110 NIDA-funded researchers and 145 other experts on drug use with access to about 250,000 people at risk for drug misuse, offered $75 for each completed questionnaire (average response 48.7% over 20 quarters); a subcommittee classified every report with DSM-IV-based ratings. No group of people who stopped tramadol without withdrawal, or who stopped another opioid, was studied (editors' reading of the design).

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_senay_2003 (JBI, high): reports someone chose to make, to the manufacturer, the FDA or an informant network paid per questionnaire (average response 48.7%), of unknown completeness; much information missing (age known for 139 of 455, dose for 63 to 78 in 100, exposure for about half); the 'atypical' category created during the study and every case rescored without a check of agreement between raters; reports with drug-seeking moved to 'abuse'; no statistical analysis; funded by the manufacturer. The shares and descriptions could be materially wrong.

inconsistency.note: One series; the Iranian case report titled as psychosis after stopping tramadol does not conflict with it.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: the claim describes what reports contained and says that neither a frequency nor a comparison with other opioids was measured. A claim that tramadol withdrawal differs from that of other opioids would be rated lower.

imprecision.note: 422 rated reports (55 atypical) are enough to describe the reported pattern; the claim gives no frequency to be precise about.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; one surveillance programme reporting every case it classified.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive (what reported cases contained): starts low; down two levels for risk of bias; very low. Status single study: one surveillance series; the Iranian review adds two case reports and no study of how often withdrawal follows stopping. The rates per 100,000 are reported cases over estimated prescriptions, with a capture the authors themselves put at about 10 in 100 or less, so they are given only as minimums. Whether the 'atypical' symptoms are particular to tramadol was not tested: no group stopping another opioid was studied; and the abstract's nearly 40% is 33 in 100 by Table 3. Not read: the committee's earlier report on the same programme (Cicero et al., 1999, Drug and Alcohol Dependence 57, 7–22) and Raffa et al. (1992) on tramadol's mechanisms.
